Gradient Boosting and K-means on the I-SPY Breast Cancer Trial

We will analyze data from the Investigation of Serial Studies to Predict Your Therapeutic Response with Imaging and moLecular Analysis (I-SPY TRIAL) breast cancer trial. This dataset contains patients with measurements derived from MRI scans. The outcome of interest is to predict the final diameter of the tumor as measured through the MRI, which is stored in the column MRI_LD_Tfinal. We have longitudinal measurements from each patient, collected at timepoints T0, T1, T2, and Tfinal. T0 is pre-treatment. T1 is early treatment. T2 is inter-regimen. Tfinal is the final measurement.

  1. Load the iSPY1 dataset by running the following. Notice that there is a fakeSite column with values ranging from 1-8. We’ve added this column to simulate combining data from 8 different sites.
ispy_dat <- read.csv("data/ispy1doctored_site.csv")
ispy_dat$HR_HER2status <- as.factor(ispy_dat$HR_HER2status)

Boosting

We will create and evaluate a gradient boosted model that predicts MRI_LD_Tfinal using all the predictors measured before Tfinal.

  1. Hold out sites 7 and 8 for testing. Store the training data in datTrain and the test data in datTest.
datTrain <- ispy_dat[ispy_dat$fakeSite != 7 & ispy_dat$fakeSite != 8, ]
datTest <- ispy_dat[ispy_dat$fakeSite == 7 | ispy_dat$fakeSite == 8, ]
  1. Here I manually implement site-wise 3-fold cross-validation (i.e. two sites per fold) rather than using the caret package. Create vector with True and False values to split the rows in datTrain into 3 folds, where sites 1 and 2 are in the first fold, sites 3 and 4 are in the second fold, and sites 5 and 6 are in the third fold. Create a list with these three True/False vectors. 
fold1 <- c(datTrain$fakeSite == 1 | datTrain$fakeSite == 2)
fold2 <- c(datTrain$fakeSite == 3 | datTrain$fakeSite == 4)
fold3 <- c(datTrain$fakeSite == 5 | datTrain$fakeSite == 6)

foldList <- list(fold1, fold2, fold3)
  1. Load the gbm package.
library(gbm)
## Loaded gbm 2.2.2
## This version of gbm is no longer under development. Consider transitioning to gbm3, https://github.com/gbm-developers/gbm3
  1. We will select the hyperparameters for a gradient boosted model using site-wise three-fold CV. Create a function named fit_fold that takes as input the fold number fold_idx, number of trees, and interaction depth. The function will fit a gradient boosted model using gbm using the aforementioned predictors. Also exclude fakeSite. Train on all the folds except for the fold_idx-th one. The function should output the mean squared error of the fitted model on the held out fold.
    Use the folds made above. Fix the shrinkage hyperparameter in gbm as 0.01.
fit_fold <- function(fold_idx, n.trees, interaction.depth) {
    
    train_indices <- !foldList[[fold_idx]]
    test_indices <- foldList[[fold_idx]]
    
    colSubset <- c("pixelVolTfinal", "ftvPeTfinal", "fakeSite")
    excludeCols <- which(colnames(datTrain) %in% colSubset)
    
    train_data <- datTrain[train_indices, -excludeCols]
    test_data <- datTrain[test_indices, -excludeCols]

    model <- gbm(formula = MRI_LD_Tfinal ~ .,
                data = train_data,
                n.trees = n.trees, 
                interaction.depth = interaction.depth, 
                shrinkage = 0.01,
                distribution = "gaussian",
                verbose = FALSE)

    predictions <- predict(model, newdata = test_data, n.trees = n.trees)

    mse <- mean((predictions - test_data$MRI_LD_Tfinal)^2)

    return(mse)
}
  1. Using the function above, tune the number of trees and interaction depth using site-wise three-fold CV. Search over the values n.trees=100, 200, 400, 800, 1600 and interaction.depth=1, 2. Which hyperparameter values minimize the cross-validated mean squared error?
# Define hyperparameter values to search
n.trees_values <- c(100, 200, 400, 800, 1600)
interaction.depth_values <- c(1, 2)

# Create an empty data frame to store results
results <- data.frame(
    n.trees = numeric(),
    interaction.depth = numeric(),
    fold = numeric(),
    mse = numeric(),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

# For each hyperparameter combination and each fold
for (n.tree in n.trees_values) {
    for (depth in interaction.depth_values) {
        for (fold_idx in 1:length(foldList)) {
            # Get MSE for this fold and hyperparameter combination
            fold_mse <- fit_fold(fold_idx, n.tree, depth)
            
            # Add to results data frame
            results <- rbind(results, data.frame(
                n.trees = n.tree,
                interaction.depth = depth,
                fold = fold_idx,
                mse = fold_mse,
                stringsAsFactors = FALSE
            ))
        }
    }
}

# Print the number of model fits to confirm that we ran the model for all combinations
print(paste("Number of model fits:", nrow(results)))
## [1] "Number of model fits: 30"
# Calculate average MSE across folds for each hyperparameter combination
cv_results <- aggregate(mse ~ n.trees + interaction.depth, data = results, FUN = mean)
names(cv_results)[3] <- "cv_mse"
cv_results
##    n.trees interaction.depth   cv_mse
## 1      100                 1 477.1734
## 2      200                 1 403.2040
## 3      400                 1 370.6352
## 4      800                 1 381.1262
## 5     1600                 1 396.8537
## 6      100                 2 458.6229
## 7      200                 2 387.2174
## 8      400                 2 368.8736
## 9      800                 2 380.4739
## 10    1600                 2 400.3944
# Find the best hyperparameters
best_idx <- which.min(cv_results$cv_mse)
best_params <- cv_results[best_idx, ]
best_params
##   n.trees interaction.depth   cv_mse
## 8     400                 2 368.8736

The hyperparameters that minimize the cross-validated mean squared error are n.trees = 400, interaction.depth = 2, with a MSE of ~ 368.876

  1. Plot the cross-validated error with respect to n.trees for the interaction depth that attained the lowest CV error.
library(ggplot2)

# Find the best interaction depth from the aggregated results
best_depth <- cv_results[which.min(cv_results$cv_mse), "interaction.depth"]

# Plot cross-validated error with respect to n.trees for the best interaction depth
ggplot(subset(cv_results, interaction.depth == best_depth), aes(x = n.trees, y = cv_mse)) +
  geom_line(color = "blue") +
  geom_point(color = "blue") +
  geom_point(data = subset(cv_results, interaction.depth == best_depth & n.trees == best_params$n.trees), 
             color = "red", size = 3) +
  labs(x = "Number of Trees", y = "Mean Squared Error",
       title = paste("Cross-Validated Error for Interaction Depth =", best_depth)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(100, 200, 400, 800, 1600), trans = "log2") +
  theme_minimal()

  1. Refit the gradient boosted model on all the training data (datTrain) using the hyperparameters that minimized the CV error.
colSubset <- c("pixelVolTfinal", "ftvPeTfinal", "fakeSite")
excludeCols <- which(colnames(datTrain) %in% colSubset)
    
datTrainFit <- datTrain[-excludeCols]

fitTest <- gbm(formula = MRI_LD_Tfinal ~ .,
                data = datTrain,
                n.trees = best_params$n.trees, 
                interaction.depth = best_params$interaction.depth, 
                shrinkage = 0.01, 
                distribution = "gaussian",
                verbose = FALSE)
  1. Evaluate the MSE of the fitted model on the test data. How much of the variance have we explained using the GBM?
# Make predictions on the test data using the model trained on all training data
predictions <- predict(fitTest, newdata = datTest, n.trees = best_params$n.trees)

# Calculate MSE on test data
test_mse <- mean((predictions - datTest$MRI_LD_Tfinal)^2)
print(paste("Test MSE:", test_mse))
## [1] "Test MSE: 399.101674177638"
# Calculate the total variance in the test data
total_variance <- var(datTest$MRI_LD_Tfinal)

# Calculate Proportion of variance explained
r_squared <- 1 - (test_mse / total_variance)
r_squared
## [1] 0.5321572

The GBM model explains 0.5321 proportion of the varience compared to just using the mean as a predictor. We’ve explained 53.21 % of the variance.

Kmeans

Let’s perform K-means on the iSPY data.

  1. Create a new data frame named ispy_subdat that only contains the continuous variables measured before Tfinal.
ispy_subdat <- read.csv("data/ispy1doctored_site.csv")
ispy_subdat$HR_HER2status <- as.factor(ispy_subdat$HR_HER2status)

# Define columns to exclude (factors, variables after Tfinal)
categoricalCols <- c("HR_HER2status", "fakeSite", "race")
tFinalCols <- grep("Tfinal", colnames(ispy_subdat), value = TRUE)
excludeCols <- c(categoricalCols, tFinalCols)

ispy_subdat <- ispy_subdat[,!names(ispy_subdat) %in% excludeCols]
  1. Before we run K-means, center and scale all the variables so that they have mean 0 and variance 1 (hint: use the scale command).
ispy_subdatScaled <- scale(ispy_subdat)
  1. Tune the number of clusters used in K-means. To do this, use the function fviz_nbclust from the factoextra library. The function fviz_nbclust determines and visualizes the optimal number of clusters using different methods (within cluster sums of squares, average silhouette and gap statistics). Plot the average silhouette with respect to the number of clusters by passing in the argument method="silhouette". What is the optimal number of clusters according to the silhouette statistic?
library(factoextra)
## Welcome! Want to learn more? See two factoextra-related books at https://goo.gl/ve3WBa
model <- fviz_nbclust(ispy_subdatScaled, method = "silhouette", FUNcluster = kmeans)
plot(model)

The optimal number of clusters according to the silhouette statistic is 3.

  1. Refit k-means using the optimal number of clusters with 15 random initializations. Use the function fviz_cluster() to plot the clusters from K-means. Observations are represented by points in the plot, using principal components if \(p > 2\). An ellipse is drawn around each cluster.
library(factoextra)
k.max <- 3

# 15 random initializations
kMeansModel <- kmeans(ispy_subdatScaled, centers = k.max, nstart = 15)

# Visualize the clusters
fviz_cluster(kMeansModel, data = ispy_subdatScaled,
             cluster = kMeansModel$cluster,
             geom = "point",     
             ellipse.type = "norm",  
             main = paste("K-means Clustering (k =", k.max, ")"))

  1. Plot the distribution of MRI_LD_Tfinal for each cluster created by K-means. How do they differ across the clusters?
# Directly assign cluster to each observation
ispy_dat$cluster <- NA  

# Make sure we have the same number of rows in both datasets
print(paste("Rows in ispy_subdat:", nrow(ispy_subdat)))
## [1] "Rows in ispy_subdat: 134"
print(paste("Rows in ispy_dat:", nrow(ispy_dat)))
## [1] "Rows in ispy_dat: 134"
# Assign clusters directly by position (assuming same order)
ispy_dat$cluster[1:nrow(ispy_subdat)] <- kMeansModel$cluster

# Check if assignment worked
print(table(ispy_dat$cluster, useNA = "ifany"))
## 
##  1  2  3 
## 17 30 87
# Plot the distribution of MRI_LD_Tfinal for each cluster
# Filter out NA values for the plot
plot_data <- subset(ispy_dat, !is.na(cluster))

# Box plot
ggplot(plot_data, aes(x = factor(cluster), y = MRI_LD_Tfinal, fill = factor(cluster))) +
  stat_boxplot(geom = "errorbar", width = 0.3) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.shape = 16, outlier.size = 2) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  labs(title = "Distribution of MRI_LD_Tfinal by Cluster",
       x = "Cluster",
       y = "MRI_LD_Tfinal",
       fill = "Cluster") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5, size = 14),
    axis.title = element_text(size = 12),
    legend.position = "right"
  )

# Make a table of summary statistics for each cluster
summary_table <- aggregate(MRI_LD_Tfinal ~ cluster, data = plot_data, 
                          FUN = function(x) c(mean = mean(x), sd = sd(x)))
print(summary_table)
##   cluster MRI_LD_Tfinal.mean MRI_LD_Tfinal.sd
## 1       1           13.35294         13.77471
## 2       2           63.23333         33.48050
## 3       3           21.47126         18.68953

Cluster 1 had an avergage MRI_LD_Tfinal of 13.35, cluster 2 had an average of 63.23, and cluster 3 had an average MRI_LD_Tfinal of 21.47. MR_LD_Tfinal is a measure of the longest value of tumor diameter at the final timepoint. This tells us that cluster 2 had a group with larger on average tumor diameter at the final timepoint. In other words, cluster 2 had the highest on average value, cluster 1 had the lowest, and cluster 3 was in the middle but was more similar to cluster 1. Cluster 2 also had the widest range of values, but were all on average higher than any of the values is cluster 1 or 3. Cluster 1 and 3 had overlap in range between ~0-13 units.
